t: Stonehenge was built and rebuilt over some 1,500 years, from an earthwork of about 3100 BCE to the sarsen circle of 2600 to 2400 BCE and later rearrangements of the bluestones.
It was a place of burial from its beginnings, and its builders moved bluestones some 140 to 150 miles from the Preseli Hills in Wales.
Its purpose remains debated: an observatory, a place of healing, a domain of the dead linked to Durrington Walls, or a symbol of unity.
dyk: Cecil Chubb bought Stonehenge at auction in 1915 for £6,600, reportedly on a whim because he believed a local man should own it, and gave it to the nation three years later.
ev: The first monument, a circular bank and ditch with the ring of Aubrey holes, was dug
The builders abandoned timber for stone and set up bluestones in the centre of the site
The great circle of sarsen stones and the trilithon horseshoe were raised
The Y and Z Holes, the last known construction at the site, were dug
John Aubrey examined the site and recorded the pits that bear his name
The Ancient Monuments Protection Act made it a legally protected monument
Cecil Chubb bought the site at auction and gave it to the nation three years later
Stonehenge and its surroundings were added to the list of World Heritage Sites

f.made: Neolithic and Bronze Age communities of southern Britain, over at least 1,500 years; the builders of the first phases descended mainly from early farmers who reached Britain about 4000 BCE, and the Bell Beaker people arrived during the megalithic phase
f.form: A circular bank and ditch about 110 m across; an outer circle of sarsen uprights about 4 m high joined by lintels with mortise and tenon joints; five trilithons in a horseshoe; rings and settings of smaller bluestones from Wales
f.where: Salisbury Plain, two miles west of Amesbury, Wiltshire; owned by the Crown Estate and managed by English Heritage, the surrounding land owned by the National Trust
f.known: The solstice alignment; the sarsen circle and trilithons; bluestones brought from the Preseli Hills; the Aubrey holes and early cremation burials; the debate over its purpose; Merlin in Geoffrey of Monmouth's legend; a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986
